The REPL now shows you the code you are typing.

### Colour

| | |
|---|---|
| syntax — `define`, `if`, `lambda`, `cond`, … | magenta |
| the interpreter's procedures — `+`, `car`, `display`, … | cyan |
| string, character and comment text | green, grey |
| a bracket that closes nothing | **red** |

Both name lists come from the machine itself rather than from a table written
out by hand: the syntax names are the interpreter's own `specialForms` keys and
the procedures are a snapshot of its builtin frame, so a name is coloured as
what it really is, and a name that does not exist is not coloured at all.

Colour is off when `TERM` is unset or `dumb`, when `NO_COLOR` is set, or when
the output is not a terminal — escapes written into a pipe or a file are noise.
If your shell exports `NO_COLOR` (this project's development shell does), the
REPL will look plain until you `unset NO_COLOR`.

### Bracket matching

The bracket the cursor is on, and the one that matches it, are drawn in bold.
The cursor counts as being on a bracket when it sits on one *or* immediately
past one — which is where it is after typing `)` or stepping over `(` — because
that is where it is most of the time.

Matching follows the reader: a bracket inside a string, a character literal
(`#\(`) or a comment is text, not structure.  A bracket left open at the end of
the line is not an error — half a form is the normal state of a REPL line — but
a closing bracket that closes nothing is, and is red.

A submitted line keeps the colours that say what the text *is* and loses the one
that says where the cursor *is*: the bracket pair is redrawn plain, because the
cursor has moved on, while `define` stays a keyword and `+` stays a procedure.
(Before this the line above stayed lit — the brackets you had just matched kept
their colour while you typed the next line; the first fix went too far and
dropped every colour instead.)

### `Error:` is red

On a terminal that takes colour, the word is red and the message is not: the
message is text a program may be reading, and a failure should be visible
without turning the error into decoration.

### Ctrl-C abandons the form it interrupted

It printed `^C` and returned to the prompt, but the evaluation was running in
another goroutine and nothing stopped it.  A form that had been "cancelled"
went on running: `(chan-send! ch 'hello)` abandoned with Ctrl-C was still parked
on the channel, and the next `(chan-recv! ch)` took `hello` from it.  The
machine now watches a channel that Ctrl-C closes, so the evaluation stops at its
next step and wakes out of a blocked send or receive.  The REPL waits for it to
notice before printing the next prompt, so the form after an interrupted one
starts from a quiet machine.

### A program that waits, waits

A program blocked on a channel nobody will ever send to used to end in a Go
runtime message — `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` — and a
stack dump about the interpreter rather than the program.  The runtime decides
that when every goroutine is asleep, so the interpreter now parks one goroutine
for the life of the process and the check never fires: a blocked program blocks,
on every path (a script, a `.scmc` file, the REPL), and Ctrl-C abandons it in the
REPL.  A Go panic anywhere is reported as an `Error:` line rather than a stack
trace.

### Also

`channel-open?`, the alias `chan-open?` replaced in 2.6.0, is gone, and `Tab`
completes a unique candidate silently, rings the bell when there is nothing to
complete, and lists several candidates only on the second press within a second.
